statement: Most complex human traits (height, performance, longevity, body weight) are highly polygenic to omnigenic: thousands of common variants each contribute tiny effects, so single-gene 'fitness/longevity/trait genes' read off a consumer chip have negligible individual predictive value.
effect_size: For a typical complex trait, heritability is spread across ~thousands of loci; 'core' genes carry a minority of it. Marquee variants (e.g. ACTN3 R577X) explain ~1-3% of performance variance.

provenance.primary: Boyle, Li & Pritchard — 'An Expanded View of Complex Traits: From Polygenic to Omnigenic', Cell 2017

confidence_notes: The foundational reason DTC 'fitness/nutrition' single-gene reports are noise for an individual. Mechanism/theory tier; not an outcome claim.

statement: The APOE-epsilon4 allele is the strongest common genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease, with a gene-dose effect: one copy raises lifetime risk roughly 2-3x and two copies roughly 8-15x versus epsilon3/epsilon3; the effect is modified by sex (larger in women) and ancestry (smaller in some African-ancestry groups).
effect_size: OR ~2-3x per epsilon4 (heterozygous), ~8-15x homozygous (Farrer epsilon4/epsilon4 OR 14.9, 95% CI 10.8-20.6 in Caucasians); effect attenuated in African ancestry, amplified in women (Farrer 1997 meta).
population: Meta-analysis across 40+ studies, multiple ancestries (Farrer 1997); original gene-dose Corder 1993

provenance.primary: Farrer, Cupples, Haines et al. — 'Effects of age, sex, and ethnicity on the association between APOE genotype and Alzheimer disease', JAMA 1997; Corder et al. Science 1993

confidence_notes: Robust ASSOCIATION (case-control/meta). A risk allele, NOT a diagnosis: most AD patients are not epsilon4 homozygous, and many epsilon4/epsilon4 carriers never develop dementia. Predictor, not lever.

statement: APOE-epsilon4 is a strong predictor with no genotype-specific therapy: there is no proven intervention that neutralizes epsilon4 risk, so disclosure carries counseling, right-not-to-know, and insurance harms, while the only available levers are the generic dementia-risk-reduction measures that benefit everyone (possibly more in epsilon4 carriers).
effect_size: No epsilon4-specific pharmacologic lever validated; generic levers (BP/lipid control, exercise, hearing correction, sleep) apply regardless of genotype.

provenance.primary: REVEAL APOE-disclosure studies (Green et al.) + dementia risk-reduction literature; manual section 08
provenance.surfaced_via: section 18 PART A synthesis; cross-ref section 08

confidence_notes: The cleanest predictor-not-lever case in practical genetics. The 'epsilon4 carriers benefit more from lifestyle' angle is suggestive, not settled. Treat as counseling guidance, not an outcome claim.

statement: Lipoprotein(a) level is largely genetically determined by the LPA locus, and genetic variants raising Lp(a) causally raise risk of coronary heart disease (and aortic stenosis), as shown by Mendelian randomization - making a one-time Lp(a) measurement a high-value, lifelong-risk test.
effect_size: LPA variants associated with both Lp(a) level and CHD in a dose-consistent (causal) pattern; ~20% of people have clinically elevated Lp(a).
population: Mendelian-randomization / large association studies (Clarke 2009, PROCARDIS, European ancestry)

provenance.primary: Clarke, Peden, Watkins et al. — 'Genetic variants associated with Lp(a) lipoprotein level and coronary disease', NEJM 2009

confidence_notes: One of the few common-variant findings that clears the cohort-not-RCT bar via Mendelian randomization (genetics as a natural experiment). Cross-ref Domain L. Note: Lp(a)-LOWERING outcome trials are still pending - causal risk factor != proven drug target yet.

statement: Testing for common MTHFR polymorphisms (C677T, A1298C) is NOT recommended for the general or healthy population: the ACMG found no evidence of utility for recurrent pregnancy loss or thrombophilia, the variants are very common, and homocysteine-lowering RCTs failed to reduce cardiovascular events - the popular 'MTHFR causes X, treat with methylfolate' narrative is unsupported.
effect_size: C677T TT genotype present in ~10-15% of many populations; modest homocysteine elevation only; homocysteine-lowering trials null for CVD events.
population: ACMG practice guideline synthesizing clinical evidence (human)

provenance.primary: Hickey, Curry, Toriello (ACMG) — 'ACMG Practice Guideline: lack of evidence for MTHFR polymorphism testing', Genet Med 2013

confidence_notes: DEBUNK. The single most overhyped variant in consumer/functional-medicine genetics. Mechanism (mild folate-cycle effect) is real and small; the marketed outcomes and special 'methylated' supplement upsell are not supported. Clean mechanism-not-outcome failure.

statement: HFE C282Y homozygosity (the commonest hereditary-hemochromatosis genotype) has low clinical penetrance: only a minority develop iron-overload disease (~28% of men, <2% of women in the HealthIron cohort), so a positive genotype is a reason to monitor iron studies, not a diagnosis - and the treatment (phlebotomy) is decided on ferritin/transferrin saturation, not the SNP.
effect_size: Iron-overload-related disease in ~28.4% of male and ~1.2% of female C282Y homozygotes over ~12y follow-up.
population: HealthIron / Melbourne Collaborative Cohort, C282Y homozygotes vs controls

provenance.primary: Allen, Gurrin, Olynyk et al. — 'Iron-overload-related disease in HFE hereditary hemochromatosis', NEJM 2008

confidence_notes: Illustrates 'a Mendelian disease that mostly doesn't happen' - genotype != phenotype. Actionable (cheap monitoring + curative phlebotomy) but the lever is the iron blood test, not the variant. Predictor-not-lever.

statement: The ACMG Secondary Findings list (SF v3.2, 81 genes) operationally defines 'actionable' genetics: highly penetrant, medically actionable conditions (hereditary cancers, familial hypercholesterolemia, cardiomyopathies/arrhythmias, aortopathies, malignant hyperthermia) worth reporting opportunistically from clinical sequencing.
effect_size: 81 genes meeting penetrance + actionability criteria (SF v3.2, 2023).

provenance.primary: Miller, Lee, Abul-Husn et al. (ACMG) — 'ACMG SF v3.2 list for reporting of secondary findings in clinical exome and genome sequencing', Genet Med 2023

confidence_notes: The professional yardstick for 'which genetic findings are worth acting on'. Anything not at roughly this penetrance-plus-action caliber is information, not a lever. Consensus/protocol tier.

statement: Pharmacogenomic variants (CYP2C19, CYP2D6, DPYD, TPMT/NUDT15, SLCO1B1, HLA-B*57:01, HLA-B*15:02) are the highest-value 'health' genetics for most people: single large-effect variants with defined clinical actions (change drug or dose), codified in CPIC guidelines - several (DPYD, TPMT, HLA-B) prevent severe or fatal toxicity.
effect_size: Examples: CYP2C19 LoF -> reduced clopidogrel efficacy (alternative agent advised); HLA-B*57:01 -> abacavir hypersensitivity (testing mandatory); DPYD deficiency -> fluoropyrimidine toxicity risk.
population: CPIC guideline evidence base (RCT + pharmacogenetic cohorts, human)

provenance.primary: CPIC guidelines (cpicpgx.org); framework Relling & Klein, Clin Pharmacol Ther 2011 (10.1038/clpt.2011.34); clopidogrel Lee et al. 2022
provenance.surfaced_via: section 18 PART A; CPIC canonical guidelines

confidence_notes: The genuinely useful clinical genetics: large effect + defined action. Strength varies by gene-drug pair (HLA-B*57:01/abacavir and DPYD among the strongest). DOI cited for clopidogrel guideline; framework Relling & Klein 2011 from canonical literature.

statement: Pre-specified 'diet-responsive' genotype patterns do NOT predict which healthy diet (low-fat vs low-carbohydrate) produces more weight loss: in the DIETFITS RCT (>600 adults) genotype-diet matching had no effect, refuting 'eat for your genotype / DNA-based diet' claims.
effect_size: No significant genotype x diet interaction on 12-month weight change; both diets produced similar (modest) average loss.
population: DIETFITS RCT, 609 overweight adults randomized, pre-genotyped

provenance.primary: Gardner, Trepanowski, King et al. — 'Effect of Low-Fat vs Low-Carbohydrate Diet on 12-Month Weight Loss... and Association With Genotype Pattern or Insulin Secretion', JAMA 2018

confidence_notes: Strongest direct test of personalized-by-genotype dieting; negative. 'DNA-based diet' products are not supported. RCT tier.

statement: FTO genotype (the 'obesity gene') does NOT modify weight-loss response to dietary, physical-activity, or drug interventions: across a meta-analysis of 9,563 individuals, carriers and non-carriers lost equivalent weight - so the FTO risk allele is no barrier to, and no special protocol for, weight loss.
effect_size: No significant difference in intervention-induced weight loss by FTO rs9939609 genotype (8 RCTs, n=9,563).
population: Meta-analysis of randomized weight-loss intervention trials

provenance.primary: Livingstone, Celis-Morales, Mathers et al. — 'FTO genotype and weight loss: systematic review and meta-analysis of 9563 individual participant data', BMJ 2016

confidence_notes: FTO predicts higher average body weight (real association) but is NOT a lever for tailoring weight-loss strategy. Predictor != lever, in the most-cited 'obesity gene'. Meta tier.

statement: Polygenic risk scores stratify disease risk at the population level but have limited individual accuracy and transfer poorly across ancestries (trained mostly on European-ancestry data), and prediction accuracy varies even WITHIN an ancestry group - so consumer 'polygenic scores' are population instruments, not validated personal predictors, and naive deployment could widen health disparities.
effect_size: PRS prediction accuracy substantially lower in non-European ancestries; meaningful within-ancestry variation by age/SES/environment.
population: Methods studies on PRS portability (UK Biobank + multi-ancestry, human)

provenance.primary: Martin, Kanai, Kamatani et al. — 'Clinical use of current polygenic risk scores may exacerbate health disparities', Nat Genet 2019; Mostafavi et al., eLife 2020
provenance.surfaced_via: section 18 PART A; canonical PRS-portability literature (Mostafavi eLife 10.7554/eLife.48376)

confidence_notes: Tempers PRS hype: real at population scale, weak and ancestry-biased at the individual level. DOIs from canonical literature (Martin 2019; Mostafavi 2020). Mechanism/methods tier.

statement: Consumer-genomics 'wellness / fitness / nutrition' reports (endurance-vs-power type, 'ideal diet', vitamin/caffeine 'needs') read small-effect common variants explaining a rounding error of polygenic traits and are entertainment-grade, not decision-grade; their relative-risk framing without absolute risk routinely misleads.
effect_size: Marquee fitness variants explain low-single-digit percent of trait variance; absolute risks often tiny even at elevated relative risk.
population: Inference from polygenicity (Boyle 2017) + DTC product reality (human)

provenance.primary: Synthesis: Boyle/Li/Pritchard omnigenic 2017 (10.1016/j.cell.2017.05.038) + DIETFITS 2018 + FTO 2016; section 18 PART A

confidence_notes: DEBUNK rooted in polygenicity + the negative diet-genotype trials. The good DTC uses (ancestry, carrier status, some PGx, a few clinically-confirmable actionable variants) are real and distinct from the wellness-report noise.

statement: A consumer-chip result tests only pre-selected spots (e.g. 3 Ashkenazi BRCA founder variants out of thousands), so a 'negative' rules out only those variants and is not clinical clearance; conversely, rare 'pathogenic' calls from raw DTC data have a high false-positive rate and must be confirmed in a diagnostic lab before any action.
effect_size: Genotyping chips read common SNPs, not whole genes; raw-data third-party 'pathogenic' findings show high false-positive rates on clinical confirmation.

provenance.primary: FDA 23andMe BRCA authorization (3 founder variants, 2018) + clinical-confirmation literature on DTC raw-data false positives; section 18 PART A

confidence_notes: Operational safety rule for DTC results: treat actionable outputs as leads to confirm, never as endpoints; never read a negative as an all-clear, especially against family history. Protocol/mechanism tier.

statement: Consumer methylation-age ('epigenetic clock') tests are not validated personal surrogates: no aging biomarker yet reliably moves with an intervention AND predicts its clinical benefit (consortium consensus), original clocks have poor test-retest reliability (many 'age-reversal' results sit within measurement noise), and different clocks disagree - so the number is a weakly-reliable correlate, not a personal aging dashboard.
effect_size: Original-clock ICC as low as ~0.6-0.8; clocks correlate imperfectly; no validated surrogate status (Moqri 2023 consensus).

provenance.primary: Moqri, Herzog, Gladyshev et al. — Biomarkers of aging consensus, Cell 2023 (10.1016/j.cell.2023.08.003); Higgins-Chen et al. Nat Aging 2022

confidence_notes: Practical-layer reframing of Domain C's clock claims: predictor (cohort) != validated surrogate, and the consumer test is noisy at the individual level. Act on validated Domain L biomarkers instead.
dedup_note: Same finding as canonical claim 'biological-age-tests-not-validated-surrogate' (Biological-age clocks not validated as a personal surrogate endpoint); retained for chapter coverage, not counted as an independent claim.

statement: Heritability is a population-variance statement, not a personal forecast or a ceiling: lifespan (~10-25% heritable) and exercise trainability (~47% heritable) describe between-person spread in a given environment, not how fixed an individual's outcome is - and changing the environment (e.g. higher training dose for apparent non-responders) still moves the outcome.
effect_size: HERITAGE: identical 20-week program -> VO2max gains 0% to >40%, training-response heritability ~47%; Montero & Lundby: 'non-responders' respond at higher dose.

provenance.primary: Bouchard et al. HERITAGE (10.1152/jappl.1999.87.3.1003); Montero & Lundby J Physiol 2017 (10.1113/JP273480)

confidence_notes: The gene x environment spine of Part A: genes load the gun, environment pulls the trigger. Genetics shapes the dose-response curve you're on but does not lock the outcome; the lever (change the stimulus) still works.
